properties.description:
What happened?

Between 17:45 UTC and 18:46 UTC on 17 August 2026, a platform issue affected Azure Monitor in West Europe. Affected customers may have experienced intermittent failures when retrieving metric data for Azure Monitor workspaces or custom metrics. This included queries made through the Azure portal or programmatically through Azure Monitor APIs and Prometheus (PromQL) queries. Some metric alerts may not have activated as expected.


What went wrong, and why?

A software defect within one component of the metrics service, responsible for processing and serving customer metric data, caused the component to become unavailable. The issue occurred during an internal service reconfiguration, where the defect prevented the affected component from recovering as designed and significantly delayed its return to normal operation. As a result, the affected portion of the service remained unavailable for longer than expected, causing query failures for customers whose requests depended on the impacted metric data.

Under normal circumstances, the service would automatically transition workloads to healthy backup infrastructure to minimize customer impact. However, planned maintenance was simultaneously taking place on the infrastructure designated for automatic failover, preventing automatic recovery from completing as designed and requiring engineering intervention.

Once customer impact was confirmed, we paused the maintenance activity, verified the backup infrastructure was healthy, and manually transitioned the workload to restore service. Once the transition was complete, affected customer metric queries returned to normal operation.


How did we respond?

  • 17:45 UTC on 17 August 2026 - Customer impact began.
  • 18:02 UTC on 17 August 2026 - Internal service telemetry detected elevated failure rates, and engineers began investigating.
  • 18:17 UTC on 17 August 2026 - The system determined that the outage criteria had been met, declared an outage, and sent initial communications to impacted customers.
  • 18:45 UTC on 17 August 2026 - After confirming the health of alternate capacity, engineers initiated a service failover to move query traffic away from the affected capacity.
  • 18:46 UTC on 17 August 2026 - Query availability returned to expected levels, and customer impact ended.


How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

  • We have optimized the affected component's recovery process, to improve recovery times and reduce the duration of impact during similar service events. (Completed)
  • We have improved our instrumentation related to background processing, to accelerate detection and diagnosis of similar issues in the future. (Completed)
  • We have updated our troubleshooting procedures, to improve identification of process blocking conditions and to provide faster mitigation guidance for engineers responding to similar events. (Completed)
  • We are optimizing our internal recovery operations, to reduce the amount of time required for affected service components to return to normal operation following service reconfiguration activities. (Estimated completion: November 2026)


How can customers make incidents like this less impactful?

  • Consider reviewing Azure multi-region design patterns and guidance for regions and availability zones when designing critical workloads: https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/architecture/patterns/geodes and https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/well-architected/design-guides/regions-availability-zones 
  • Consider evaluating the reliability of your applications using guidance from the Azure Well-Architected Framework and its interactive Well-Architected Review: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/WAF 
  • The impact times above represent the full incident duration and are not specific to any individual customer. Actual impact varied between customers and resources. For guidance on implementing monitoring to understand granular impact, refer to https://aka.ms/AzPIR/Monitoring
  • Consider ensuring that the right people in your organization receive notifications about future service issues by configuring Azure Service Health alerts: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/Alerts


How can we make our incident communications more useful?

You can rate this PIR and provide any feedback using our quick 3-question survey: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/TJGB-WGG

What happened?

Between 17:45 UTC and 18:46 UTC on 17 August 2026, a platform issue affected Azure Monitor in West Europe. Affected customers may have experienced intermittent failures when retrieving metric data for Azure Monitor workspaces or custom metrics. This included queries made through the Azure portal or programmatically through Azure Monitor APIs and Prometheus (PromQL) queries. Some metric alerts may not have activated as expected.


What went wrong, and why?

A software defect within one component of the metrics service, responsible for processing and serving customer metric data, caused the component to become unavailable. The issue occurred during an internal service reconfiguration, where the defect prevented the affected component from recovering as designed and significantly delayed its return to normal operation. As a result, the affected portion of the service remained unavailable for longer than expected, causing query failures for customers whose requests depended on the impacted metric data.

Under normal circumstances, the service would automatically transition workloads to healthy backup infrastructure to minimize customer impact. However, planned maintenance was simultaneously taking place on the infrastructure designated for automatic failover, preventing automatic recovery from completing as designed and requiring engineering intervention.

Once customer impact was confirmed, we paused the maintenance activity, verified the backup infrastructure was healthy, and manually transitioned the workload to restore service. Once the transition was complete, affected customer metric queries returned to normal operation.


How did we respond?

  • 17:45 UTC on 17 August 2026 - Customer impact began.
  • 18:02 UTC on 17 August 2026 - Internal service telemetry detected elevated failure rates, and engineers began investigating.
  • 18:17 UTC on 17 August 2026 - The system determined that the outage criteria had been met, declared an outage, and sent initial communications to impacted customers.
  • 18:45 UTC on 17 August 2026 - After confirming the health of alternate capacity, engineers initiated a service failover to move query traffic away from the affected capacity.
  • 18:46 UTC on 17 August 2026 - Query availability returned to expected levels, and customer impact ended.


How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

  • We have optimized the affected component's recovery process, to improve recovery times and reduce the duration of impact during similar service events. (Completed)
  • We have improved our instrumentation related to background processing, to accelerate detection and diagnosis of similar issues in the future. (Completed)
  • We have updated our troubleshooting procedures, to improve identification of process blocking conditions and to provide faster mitigation guidance for engineers responding to similar events. (Completed)
  • We are optimizing our internal recovery operations, to reduce the amount of time required for affected service components to return to normal operation following service reconfiguration activities. (Estimated completion: November 2026)


How can customers make incidents like this less impactful?

  • Consider reviewing Azure multi-region design patterns and guidance for regions and availability zones when designing critical workloads: https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/architecture/patterns/geodes and https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/well-architected/design-guides/regions-availability-zones 
  • Consider evaluating the reliability of your applications using guidance from the Azure Well-Architected Framework and its interactive Well-Architected Review: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/WAF 
  • The impact times above represent the full incident duration and are not specific to any individual customer. Actual impact varied between customers and resources. For guidance on implementing monitoring to understand granular impact, refer to https://aka.ms/AzPIR/Monitoring
  • Consider ensuring that the right people in your organization receive notifications about future service issues by configuring Azure Service Health alerts: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/Alerts


How can we make our incident communications more useful?

You can rate this PIR and provide any feedback using our quick 3-question survey: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/TJGB-WGG
